title: Битва за кастрюлю  (Battle over the Soup Pot)

segments.t: Letting Sasha and Nastya out of the walk-in refrigerator fails to bring peace. That evening at the apartment, the two women clash over a broken mug that Kostya gave Nastya and argue fiercely over whose pot is sitting on the stove.
Мне вообще ничего твоего не надо.
Let's replay the exchange and look closely at each Russian phrase.
'Kostyan, just relax.' Max anchors the line on 'Kostyan', while 'you' completes the thought.
'At least they made up.' The plural past ending '-li' on the verb for 'reconciled' covers a group or the polite 'you'. Nastya answers right away.
'Kostik gave that mug to me.' In Russian, the idea of 'for me' flows naturally into 'donated' without extra filler words.
'I will buy you a new one.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'I' before landing on 'I'll give'.
'That smells so delicious.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'how' before landing on 'it smells'. Nastya answers right away.
'She did that on purpose.' The grammar packs 'she' and 'on purpose' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'You saw it yourself.' The meaning hinges on 'you' working together with 'to see' in spoken Russian.
'Why did you put it right next to the edge?' Kostya brings out the contrast between 'what for' and 'you' in a few short words. Nastya answers right away.
'What about me?' The grammar packs 'and' and 'I' into a tight, idiomatic kitchen exchange.
'Let us sit down and eat.' Notice how Russian expresses 'let's' and 'will eat' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
'I did not even use it.' The meaning hinges on 'I' working together with 'to use' in spoken Russian. Nastya answers right away.
Мне вообще ничего твоего не надо.
'I do not want anything of yours at all.' In Russian, the idea of 'for me' flows naturally into 'at' without extra filler words.
'That is my pot.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'this' before landing on 'pot'. Let's hear the complete conversation once more.
